lesson.title: How Much Data Is Enough: The Real Cost and Power of Sample Size
lesson.summary: Explains how sample size drives the precision of estimates and the power of tests through the 1 over square root of n rule, and why bigger samples are not free and do not fix everything.
lesson.body:
Every statistic you have computed this course, a sample proportion, a sample mean, the slope of a regression line, varies from sample to sample. That variability is measured by the standard error, and the standard error shrinks as sample size n grows, but not in a straight line. It shrinks proportional to 1 divided by the square root of n. You met this fact quietly, back when you first computed the standard error of a sample proportion or sample mean to build a confidence interval. It turns out to be the single idea that drives almost every practical decision about how big a study needs to be.

Because of the square root, sample size has diminishing returns. To cut a margin of error in half, you do not double the sample size, you quadruple it. This is exactly what the sample size formulas for a confidence interval capture: solving for n given a target margin of error always produces this square-and-scale relationship. The same idea drives statistical power, the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. Recall that power depends on the significance level, the true effect size, the variability in the population, and the sample size. Increasing n shrinks the standard error of the sampling distribution, which pulls the two overlapping distributions in a power diagram, the one centered at the null value and the one centered at the true value, further apart relative to their spread. That is the entire mechanism by which more data makes a real effect easier to detect.

Effect size and sample size trade off directly. A large, obvious effect, like a new medication that cuts recovery time by half, can be detected reliably with a fairly small sample. A subtle effect, like a teaching method that nudges average test scores up by a point, needs a much larger sample to reach the same power, because the true value sits much closer to the null value and the sampling distributions overlap heavily unless the standard error is squeezed down. This is why underpowered studies of subtle effects so often produce a fail to reject conclusion that gets misreported as proof of no effect, when really the study simply was not large enough to see it clearly.

It is just as important to know what sample size does not fix. A larger sample reduces random sampling variability, but it does nothing to reduce bias. Bias is a systematic error introduced by how the data was collected, not a matter of not having enough of it, and the next section of this course looks closely at that distinction. It is also worth remembering that statistical significance is not the same as practical importance. With a large enough sample, almost any nonzero difference, even a genuinely trivial one, will produce a small p-value. That is why a full report never states significance alone. It reports the estimate, a confidence interval or effect size showing how large the difference actually is, and lets the reader judge whether that size matters in context.

This same 1 over square root of n idea runs through the whole course, from planning how many people to survey, to deciding whether an experiment has enough power to be worth running, to judging how precisely a regression slope has been estimated. Recognizing it lets you both design a study well and read someone else's results critically, asking not just whether a result was significant but whether it was significant because it is real and large, or significant only because the sample was enormous.
